meta.note: Original CISSP-style practice questions. matching questions carry a prompts[] (left items numbered 1..n) and options[] (right items A..n); correct_answer encodes the pairing. sequence_ordering correct_answer lists option labels in correct order.

questions.question: The identity proofing process consists of which three core steps?

explanation.why_correct: Identity proofing consists of resolution (uniquely identifying the applicant), validation (confirming the evidence is genuine), and verification (confirming the evidence belongs to the applicant).

why_others_are_wrong.B: Encrypt/hash/sign are cryptographic operations, not proofing steps.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Detect/respond/recover are incident/CSF functions.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Plan/do/check is the Deming cycle.

questions.exam_reasoning: Recall of the three identity-proofing steps.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 5 > Identity Management Introduction > Identity Proofing Process

questions.question: Order the identity proofing process steps as described in the guide. (Provide the option labels in order.)

explanation.why_correct: The flow runs from the applicant request, to resolution, validation, verification, and finally enrollment (creating the credential).

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests the ordered identity-proofing steps.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 5 > Identity Management Introduction > Proofing Process Steps

questions.question: In identity proofing, the "resolution" step specifically aims to:

options.label: C
options.text: Uniquely distinguish the applicant from all other individuals

options.label: D
options.text: Grant the applicant access to all systems

explanation.why_correct: Resolution uniquely identifies/distinguishes the applicant as a single, specific person before evidence is validated and verified.

why_others_are_wrong.A: Encrypting a biometric template is a storage/protection step, not resolution.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Granting access is authorization, which follows enrollment.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Revoking credentials is part of deprovisioning, not proofing resolution.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests the meaning of the resolution step.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 5 > Identity Management Introduction > Proofing Process Steps

questions.question: During proofing, the "verification" step confirms that:

options.label: A
options.text: The applicant has paid for the service

options.label: C
options.text: The validated identity evidence actually belongs to the applicant presenting it

explanation.why_correct: Verification confirms that the (already validated) identity evidence genuinely relates to the applicant—linking the person to the evidence.

why_others_are_wrong.A: Payment is unrelated to identity verification.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Connection encryption is a transport concern, not proofing verification.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Password complexity is a credential policy, not identity verification.

questions.exam_reasoning: Distinguishes verification (binds evidence to applicant) from validation (evidence authenticity).

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 5 > Identity Management Introduction > Proofing Process Steps

questions.question: In identity management, increasing assurance levels (Level 1 to Level 3) generally indicate:

options.label: B
options.text: Progressively stronger confidence/rigor in the identity proofing and authentication

options.label: C
options.text: The physical size of the data center

options.label: D
options.text: The number of users in the system

explanation.why_correct: Higher assurance levels require more rigorous proofing and stronger authentication, providing greater confidence in the claimed identity.

why_others_are_wrong.A: Higher levels are stronger, not weaker.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Assurance levels measure confidence, not user counts.
why_others_are_wrong.C: They are unrelated to data center size.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests that higher assurance = greater rigor/confidence.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 5 > Identity Management Introduction > Assurance Levels

questions.question: A Credential Service Provider (CSP) is responsible for:

options.label: B
options.text: Physically guarding the data center entrance

options.label: C
options.text: Issuing and managing credentials for subscribers after enrollment

explanation.why_correct: A CSP registers identities and issues/manages credentials for subscribers as part of the identity lifecycle.

why_others_are_wrong.B: Physical guarding is a facility security function.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Fire suppression is a physical control.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Inter-AS routing is a BGP/router function.

questions.exam_reasoning: Recall of the CSP role.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 5 > Identity Management Introduction > Establishing Identity

questions.question: Order the identity and access provisioning lifecycle steps as described in the guide. (Provide the option labels in order.)

explanation.why_correct: The lifecycle runs from provisioning (granting access), to periodic review (re-certifying access), to revocation (removing access when no longer needed).

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests the provisioning lifecycle order.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 5 > Identity Management Introduction > Identity and Access Lifecycle

questions.question: An employee resigns. From an access-management standpoint, what is the MOST time-critical deprovisioning action?

options.label: B
options.text: Add them to additional security groups for record-keeping

options.label: C
options.text: Schedule their next access review for next quarter

options.label: D
options.text: Promptly revoke the departing employee's access to systems and data

explanation.why_correct: Access should be revoked quickly on departure to minimize the window for misuse of lingering credentials.

why_others_are_wrong.C: A future review does nothing to close the immediate access window.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Furniture handling is not an access concern.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Adding groups expands access—the opposite of deprovisioning.

questions.exam_reasoning: Prioritizes prompt access revocation in deprovisioning.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 5 > Identity Management Introduction > Deprovisioning

questions.question: Periodic access reviews (recertification) during the identity lifecycle primarily help to:

options.label: D
options.text: Detect and remove excessive or no-longer-needed access (privilege creep)

explanation.why_correct: Regular access reviews identify accumulated/unnecessary access and adjust it, countering privilege creep and unauthorized use.

why_others_are_wrong.A: Reviews right-size access; they do not add administrators.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Traffic encryption is unrelated to access review.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Reviews complement, not replace, authentication.

questions.exam_reasoning: Ties access reviews to controlling privilege creep.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 5 > Identity Management Introduction > Lifecycle Steps

questions.question: Automating the provisioning and deprovisioning process primarily improves security by:

options.label: A
options.text: Ensuring access is granted and removed consistently and promptly, reducing human error

options.label: B
options.text: Eliminating the need for any access policy

options.label: C
options.text: Guaranteeing no account is ever disabled

options.label: D
options.text: Allowing users to grant themselves any access

explanation.why_correct: Automation makes provisioning/deprovisioning consistent and timely, reducing the manual errors and delays that leave dangling access.

why_others_are_wrong.B: Automation enforces policy; it does not remove the need for one.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Self-granting access violates least privilege and separation of duties.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Automation should ensure accounts ARE disabled when appropriate.

questions.exam_reasoning: Connects automation to consistent, timely access changes.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 5 > Identity Management Introduction > Key Considerations

questions.question: Federated Identity Management (FIM) primarily enables:

options.label: A
options.text: Users to access multiple organizations' systems using a single, shared identity across trust domains

options.label: C
options.text: Encryption of all data at rest

explanation.why_correct: FIM lets a user's identity be trusted across organizational boundaries, so one identity can access resources in multiple trust domains (e.g., via SAML).

why_others_are_wrong.C: Data-at-rest encryption is a separate control.
why_others_are_wrong.D: OS patching is unrelated to federation.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Physical access control is a facility function.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests the cross-domain shared-identity purpose of FIM.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 5 > Identity Management Introduction > Federated Identity Management

questions.question: Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML) is built on XML and is primarily used to:

options.label: A
options.text: Encrypt files on a hard drive

options.label: C
options.text: Exchange authentication and authorization assertions between an identity provider and a service provider

explanation.why_correct: SAML uses XML (and SOAP) to exchange authentication/authorization assertions between an identity provider (IdP) and service provider (SP), enabling web SSO/federation.

why_others_are_wrong.D: IP assignment is DHCP's function.
why_others_are_wrong.A: File encryption is unrelated to SAML.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Fire suppression is a physical control.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps cross-domain assertion exchange to SAML.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 5 > Identity Management Introduction > Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML)

questions.question: In a SAML web-SSO flow, a user tries to access a partner web application. The application redirects to a trusted party that authenticates the user and asserts their identity. The application is the ____ and the authenticating party is the ____.

explanation.why_correct: The application consuming the assertion is the Service Provider (SP); the party that authenticates the user and issues the assertion is the Identity Provider (IdP).

why_others_are_wrong.C: This reverses the roles—the app is the SP, the authenticator is the IdP.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Resource Owner/Server are OAuth roles, not SAML SP/IdP.
why_others_are_wrong.A: KDC/TGS are Kerberos components, not SAML roles.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests SAML SP vs IdP roles in an SSO flow.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 5 > Identity Management Introduction > Operational Flow of SAML

questions.question: Service Provisioning Markup Language (SPML) is used primarily to:

options.label: A
options.text: Exchange user, resource, and service provisioning information between organizations/systems

explanation.why_correct: SPML is an XML-based standard for exchanging provisioning information (creating/managing accounts and resources) across systems.

why_others_are_wrong.D: Biometric authentication is unrelated to SPML.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Email encryption uses S/MIME/PGP, not SPML.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Packet routing is a network-layer function.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps cross-system provisioning to SPML.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 5 > Identity Management Introduction > Service Provisioning Markup Language (SPML)

questions.question: Extensible Access Control Markup Language (XACML) is primarily used to:

options.label: B
options.text: Resolve domain names to IP addresses

options.label: D
options.text: Define and evaluate attribute-based access control policies

explanation.why_correct: XACML is a standard for expressing and evaluating access control policies, commonly underpinning attribute-based access control (ABAC/PBAC).

why_others_are_wrong.C: Voice over IP is VoIP, unrelated to XACML.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Backup power is a UPS/generator function.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Name resolution is DNS.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps access-policy definition to XACML.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 5 > Identity Management Introduction > Extensible Access Control Markup Language (XACML)

questions.question: Match each identity/access standard (1-4) to its primary purpose (A-D).

explanation.why_correct: SAML → authn/authz assertions/SSO (B); SPML → provisioning exchange (A); XACML → access-policy definition (D); OAuth → token-based delegated authorization (C).

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests mapping of identity standards to their purposes.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 5 > Identity Management Introduction > Federated Identity Management

questions.question: A key BENEFIT of delegated identity management is that it:

options.label: B
options.text: Eliminates the need for any authentication

options.label: C
options.text: Allows identity/access administration to be distributed to appropriate parties while maintaining central policy

options.label: D
options.text: Forces every user to share one password

explanation.why_correct: Delegated identity management distributes administrative responsibility (e.g., to departments or partners) while central governance/policy is maintained, improving scalability.

why_others_are_wrong.B: Delegation does not remove authentication.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Shared passwords destroy accountability and are not delegation.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Logging remains essential; delegation does not remove it.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests the distributed-administration benefit of delegation.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 5 > Identity Management Introduction > Delegated Identity Management

questions.question: A multinational company wants consistent access policy and a single point of administration for identities across all regions. Which access-control administration approach BEST fits?

options.label: D
options.text: Fully decentralized control with no coordination

explanation.why_correct: Centralized access control provides a single administration point and consistent policy enforcement across the organization, ideal for uniform governance.

why_others_are_wrong.D: Fully decentralized control yields inconsistent policy and weaker governance for this goal.
why_others_are_wrong.B: No access control is never acceptable.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Self-administration of rights violates least privilege and separation of duties.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps a need for consistent, single-point administration to centralized access control.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 5 > Identity Management Introduction > Identity Management

questions.question: Which sequence correctly orders the core IAM concepts for a subject interacting with a system?

explanation.why_correct: A subject is first identified, then authenticated (proves the identity), then authorized (granted access), with accountability (auditing) tracking actions throughout.

why_others_are_wrong.A: Authorization cannot precede identification/authentication.
why_others_are_wrong.B: This reverses the logical order.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Identification must come before authentication.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests the identification→authentication→authorization→accountability order.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 5 > Identity Management Introduction > Identity Management

questions.question: The "validation" step of identity proofing confirms that:

options.label: A
options.text: The submitted identity evidence is authentic and accurate

options.label: B
options.text: The data center temperature is within range

options.label: C
options.text: The applicant has logged out of all sessions

options.label: D
options.text: The firewall rules are correctly ordered

explanation.why_correct: Validation confirms the identity evidence itself is genuine/accurate (e.g., a real, unexpired ID document), before verification links it to the applicant.

why_others_are_wrong.C: Logging out sessions is unrelated to proofing validation.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Temperature is an environmental control concern.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Firewall ordering is a network control, not proofing.

questions.exam_reasoning: Distinguishes validation (evidence authenticity) from verification.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 5 > Identity Management Introduction > Proofing Process Steps

questions.question: An employee transfers from Finance to Marketing. From an access-management standpoint, the BEST practice during this "mover" event is to:

options.label: B
options.text: Grant the new role's access and remove the old role's access that is no longer needed

options.label: D
options.text: Keep all Finance access and simply add Marketing access

explanation.why_correct: On role change, access should be re-baselined to the new role—adding what is needed and removing now-unneeded access—to avoid privilege creep.

why_others_are_wrong.D: Retaining old access while adding new access causes privilege creep.
why_others_are_wrong.A: A transferring employee still needs an active account for the new role.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Granting admin rights violates least privilege.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests proper handling of a mover/role-change event.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 5 > Identity Management Introduction > Identity and Access Lifecycle

questions.question: Which TWO of the following are core building blocks of SAML? (Select TWO.)

explanation.why_correct: SAML is structured around assertions (statements about a subject), protocols, and bindings (how messages are transported).

why_others_are_wrong.D: Rainbow tables are a cryptanalytic attack artifact.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Fire classes are a physical-security concept.

questions.exam_reasoning: Identifies SAML building blocks.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 5 > Identity Management Introduction > SAML Assertions, Protocols, and Bindings

questions.question: A drawback of a decentralized/distributed access control approach is that it:

options.label: A
options.text: Eliminates the need for any identity store

options.label: B
options.text: Always provides a single point of administration

options.label: D
options.text: Can lead to inconsistent policy enforcement across the organization

explanation.why_correct: Decentralized control distributes administration closer to resources but risks inconsistent policy and configuration across the organization.

why_others_are_wrong.B: A single administration point is a feature of centralized, not decentralized, control.
why_others_are_wrong.A: An identity store is still required.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Decentralization tends to produce variation, not guaranteed uniformity.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests the consistency drawback of decentralized access control.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 5 > Identity Management Introduction > Identity Management

questions.question: A password is an example of which authentication factor type?

explanation.why_correct: A password is knowledge-based (Type 1 — something you know).

why_others_are_wrong.D: Type 2 is a possession such as a token or smart card.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Type 3 is a biometric trait.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Location is a contextual factor, not a primary Type.

questions.exam_reasoning: Recall of Type 1 (knowledge) factors.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 5 > Authentication Mechanisms > Authentication Factor Types

questions.question: A hardware token or smart card represents which authentication factor type?

explanation.why_correct: A token or smart card is a possession-based factor (Type 2 — something you have).

why_others_are_wrong.B: Type 1 is knowledge (e.g., a password/PIN).
why_others_are_wrong.D: Type 3 is a biometric.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Context-based factors (e.g., location) are not Type 2.

questions.exam_reasoning: Recall of Type 2 (possession) factors.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 5 > Authentication Mechanisms > Authentication Factor Types

questions.question: A fingerprint scan is which authentication factor type?

explanation.why_correct: A fingerprint is a biometric trait (Type 3 — something you are).

why_others_are_wrong.B: Type 1 is knowledge-based.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Type 2 is possession-based.
why_others_are_wrong.C: "Something you do" (e.g., keystroke dynamics) is a behavioral/contextual factor, not the physiological Type 3 fingerprint.

questions.exam_reasoning: Recall of Type 3 (biometric) factors.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 5 > Authentication Mechanisms > Authentication Factor Types

questions.question: For authentication to qualify as TRUE multi-factor authentication (MFA), the factors used must:

options.label: A
options.text: Be entered on the same screen

options.label: B
options.text: All be biometrics from the same finger

options.label: C
options.text: Come from two or more DIFFERENT factor types (e.g., something you know + something you have)

options.label: D
options.text: All be passwords of different lengths

explanation.why_correct: MFA requires factors from different categories (knowledge, possession, inherence); combining two of the same type (e.g., two passwords) is not true MFA.

why_others_are_wrong.D: Two passwords are both Type 1—still single-factor in nature.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Two biometrics are both Type 3, not multi-factor.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Where factors are entered is irrelevant to whether they are different types.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests that MFA needs distinct factor types.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 5 > Authentication Mechanisms > Types of Authentication Factors

questions.question: A login requires a password AND a one-time code from a hardware token. How many DISTINCT factor types are in use, and what is this called?

explanation.why_correct: A password (Type 1, know) plus a token code (Type 2, have) uses two different factor types—two-factor authentication.

why_others_are_wrong.D: Two different types is not single-factor.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Only two types are used, not three.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Authentication is occurring, so it is not anonymous.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests counting distinct factor types for 2FA.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 5 > Authentication Mechanisms > Authentication Process Examples

questions.question: Match each authentication factor category (1-4) to an example (A-D).

options.label: B
options.text: A login restricted to a trusted geographic location

options.label: D
options.text: A smart card or hardware token

explanation.why_correct: Know → password/PIN (B); Have → smart card/token (A); Are → fingerprint/iris (D); Somewhere you are → geographic/location-based (C).

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests mapping of factor categories to examples.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 5 > Authentication Mechanisms > Authentication Factor Types

questions.question: Evaluating a login's geographic location and the time of day as part of the access decision is an example of:

explanation.why_correct: Context-based authentication factors in attributes like location ("somewhere you are"), time, and behavior to strengthen or adapt access decisions.

why_others_are_wrong.A: Knowledge-only authentication ignores contextual signals.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Static packet filtering is a firewall technique.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Key escrow is a key-management control.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps location/time signals to context-based authentication.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 5 > Authentication Mechanisms > Context-Based Authentication

questions.question: A bank wants to strengthen logins against stolen passwords. Which change provides the GREATEST improvement to authentication assurance?

options.label: A
options.text: Add a second factor of a different type (e.g., a possession-based token or biometric)

options.label: C
options.text: Display the password as the user types it

options.label: D
options.text: Ask the same security question twice

explanation.why_correct: Adding a different factor type (possession or inherence) means a stolen password alone is insufficient—materially raising assurance versus knowledge-only changes.

why_others_are_wrong.B: A longer password is still a single knowledge factor that can be phished/stolen.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Repeating a knowledge question adds no new factor type.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Revealing the typed password weakens, not strengthens, security.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests that adding a distinct factor type best mitigates stolen-password risk.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 5 > Authentication Mechanisms > Key Exam Tips

questions.question: Which of the following is a BEHAVIORAL biometric rather than a physiological one?

explanation.why_correct: Keystroke dynamics (how a person types) is a behavioral biometric; fingerprints, iris, and retina are physiological traits.

why_others_are_wrong.D: A fingerprint is a physiological trait.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Iris pattern is physiological.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Retina pattern is physiological.

questions.exam_reasoning: Distinguishes behavioral from physiological biometrics.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 5 > Authentication Mechanisms > Behavioral Attributes

questions.question: In a biometric system, the False Rejection Rate (FRR), also called a Type 1 error, occurs when the system:

options.label: A
options.text: Incorrectly REJECTS a legitimate, authorized user

explanation.why_correct: FRR (Type 1 error) is a false rejection—an authorized user is wrongly denied; it harms usability/availability.

why_others_are_wrong.B: Falsely accepting an impostor is the False Acceptance Rate (FAR, Type 2 error).
why_others_are_wrong.D: A crash is a reliability failure, not FRR.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Plaintext template storage is a protection issue, not FRR.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps false rejection of legitimate users to FRR (Type 1).

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 5 > Authentication Mechanisms > Biometric System Errors

questions.question: Which biometric error is generally the MOST dangerous from a security standpoint?

options.label: A
options.text: False Rejection Rate (FRR / Type 1) — rejecting a valid user

options.label: B
options.text: False Acceptance Rate (FAR / Type 2) — accepting an impostor

explanation.why_correct: A false acceptance (FAR, Type 2) admits an unauthorized impostor, which is the more serious security failure; FRR mainly hurts usability.

why_others_are_wrong.A: FRR denies legitimate users—an inconvenience, not a breach.
why_others_are_wrong.D: CER is a tuning metric (where FRR=FAR), not itself an error event.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Enrollment time is a usability metric, not a security error.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests that FAR (Type 2) is the security-critical biometric error.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 5 > Authentication Mechanisms > Biometric System Errors

questions.question: The Crossover Error Rate (CER), also called the Equal Error Rate (EER), is:

options.label: A
options.text: The encryption strength of stored templates

options.label: B
options.text: The time required to scan a fingerprint

options.label: C
options.text: The maximum number of users a system can enroll

options.label: D
options.text: The point where the False Rejection Rate equals the False Acceptance Rate; a lower CER indicates a more accurate system

explanation.why_correct: CER/EER is the rate at which FRR equals FAR; a lower CER means the biometric system is more accurate overall and is used to compare/tune systems.

why_others_are_wrong.C: CER is an accuracy metric, not an enrollment capacity.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Scan time is a usability metric, not CER.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Template encryption is a protection measure, not CER.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests the CER/EER definition and that lower is better.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 5 > Authentication Mechanisms > Crossover Error Rate (CER)

questions.question: A high-security facility tunes its biometric scanner to be more strict. What is the LIKELY trade-off?

options.label: A
options.text: Both FAR and FRR drop to zero automatically

options.label: B
options.text: FAR decreases (fewer impostors accepted) but FRR increases (more legitimate users rejected)

options.label: D
options.text: The CER is no longer relevant after tuning

explanation.why_correct: Tightening the threshold reduces false acceptances (lower FAR) at the cost of more false rejections (higher FRR)—the inherent biometric trade-off.

why_others_are_wrong.A: No tuning eliminates both error types simultaneously.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Stricter settings lower FAR, not raise it.
why_others_are_wrong.D: CER remains a useful comparison metric regardless of tuning.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests the FAR/FRR trade-off when adjusting sensitivity.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 5 > Authentication Mechanisms > Crossover Error Rate (CER)

questions.question: Which TWO of the following are behavioral biometrics? (Select TWO.)

explanation.why_correct: Signature dynamics and voice pattern recognition are behavioral biometrics; iris and fingerprint are physiological.

why_others_are_wrong.D: An iris scan is a physiological biometric.
why_others_are_wrong.C: A fingerprint is a physiological biometric.

questions.exam_reasoning: Identifies behavioral biometrics.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 5 > Authentication Mechanisms > Behavioral Attributes

questions.question: LDAP (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol) is primarily used to:

options.label: B
options.text: Query and manage directory services that store identity/account information

options.label: D
options.text: Suppress fires in a server room

explanation.why_correct: LDAP is used to access and manage directory services (e.g., Active Directory), which store users, groups, and other identity data.

why_others_are_wrong.A: File encryption is unrelated to LDAP.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Fire suppression is a physical control.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Backup power is a UPS/generator function.

questions.exam_reasoning: Recall of LDAP's directory-access purpose.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 5 > Authentication Mechanisms > LDAP (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol)

questions.question: In an LDAP Distinguished Name (DN), what does the "OU" component represent?

explanation.why_correct: In an LDAP DN, OU = Organizational Unit (a container/subdivision), alongside CN (Common Name) and DC (Domain Component).

why_others_are_wrong.B: "Object Username" is not an LDAP DN component.
why_others_are_wrong.C: "Outbound URL" is not an LDAP DN component.
why_others_are_wrong.A: "Open Utility" is not an LDAP DN component.

questions.exam_reasoning: Recall of the OU component in an LDAP DN.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 5 > Authentication Mechanisms > LDAP (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol)

questions.question: In an LDAP Distinguished Name, the "CN" component typically identifies the:

options.label: B
options.text: Common Name (e.g., a specific user or object)

explanation.why_correct: CN = Common Name, which identifies a specific entry such as a user or object within the directory.

why_others_are_wrong.A: "Country Number" is not an LDAP DN component.
why_others_are_wrong.D: "Cipher Name" is unrelated to LDAP DNs.
why_others_are_wrong.C: "Cache Node" is not an LDAP DN component.

questions.question: The "AAA" framework in access management stands for:

questions.question: A notable difference between TACACS+ and RADIUS is that TACACS+:

options.label: A
options.text: Encrypts the entire payload and separates authentication, authorization, and accounting

options.label: B
options.text: Is identical to RADIUS in every respect

options.label: C
options.text: Sends all data in cleartext with no encryption

options.label: D
options.text: Cannot be used for network device administration

explanation.why_correct: TACACS+ encrypts the full payload and treats authentication, authorization, and accounting as separate functions; RADIUS encrypts only the password and combines authentication/authorization.

why_others_are_wrong.C: TACACS+ encrypts the entire payload, not nothing.
why_others_are_wrong.D: TACACS+ is commonly used for administering network devices.
why_others_are_wrong.B: They differ in encryption scope and AAA separation.

questions.exam_reasoning: Distinguishes TACACS+ (full encryption, separated AAA) from RADIUS.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 5 > Authentication Mechanisms > AAA (Authentication, Authorization, and Accounting)

questions.question: Diameter is best described as:

options.label: B
options.text: A physical security barrier around a facility

options.label: C
options.text: A successor AAA protocol designed to improve upon RADIUS

explanation.why_correct: Diameter is an AAA protocol developed as an evolution/successor to RADIUS with enhanced capabilities.

why_others_are_wrong.B: Physical barriers are facility controls.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Diameter is not a biometric scanner.
why_others_are_wrong.D: It is not a fire suppression agent.

questions.exam_reasoning: Recall of Diameter as a RADIUS successor.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 5 > Authentication Mechanisms > AAA (Authentication, Authorization, and Accounting)

questions.question: The "Accounting" component of AAA is most directly associated with which security goal?

explanation.why_correct: Accounting records user activities (e.g., session start/stop, commands), supporting accountability and auditing.

why_others_are_wrong.A: Data-at-rest confidentiality is a separate control.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Perimeter defense is a physical control.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Load balancing is a performance/availability technique.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps AAA accounting to accountability/auditing.

questions.question: Single-factor authentication (SFA) using only a password is considered weak primarily because:

options.label: A
options.text: It cannot be used on modern systems

options.label: B
options.text: It requires too many devices to log in

options.label: C
options.text: It always locks out legitimate users

options.label: D
options.text: A single stolen or guessed credential grants full access

explanation.why_correct: With SFA, compromising the single factor (e.g., a phished password) is enough to gain access; MFA mitigates this.

why_others_are_wrong.B: SFA requires fewer, not more, devices.
why_others_are_wrong.C: SFA does not inherently lock out legitimate users.
why_others_are_wrong.A: SFA is still widely (if unwisely) used on modern systems.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests the single-point-of-compromise weakness of SFA.

questions.question: Which of the following is a PHYSIOLOGICAL biometric?

explanation.why_correct: A retina scan measures a physical (physiological) characteristic; the others are behavioral biometrics.

why_others_are_wrong.A: Keystroke dynamics is behavioral.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Signature dynamics is behavioral.

questions.question: In LDAP, a Distinguished Name (DN) serves to:

options.label: B

options.label: C
options.text: Uniquely identify an entry's full path within the directory hierarchy

options.label: D
options.text: Assign IP addresses to directory clients

explanation.why_correct: A DN uniquely identifies a directory entry by specifying its complete hierarchical path (e.g., CN=user,OU=Sales,DC=example,DC=com).

why_others_are_wrong.A: A DN names an entry; it does not encrypt the database.
why_others_are_wrong.D: IP assignment is DHCP's function.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Backup power is a UPS/generator function.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests the unique-path purpose of an LDAP DN.

questions.question: Analyzing the unique rhythm and timing of how a user types their password reflects which contextual/behavioral factor?

explanation.why_correct: Keystroke dynamics is a "something you do" behavioral factor based on how the user performs an action.

why_others_are_wrong.C: "Something you have" is a possession factor.
why_others_are_wrong.A: "Somewhere you are" is a location factor.
why_others_are_wrong.D: "Something you know" is the password content itself, not the typing rhythm.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps typing rhythm to "something you do".

questions.question: Which TWO combinations qualify as TRUE multi-factor authentication? (Select TWO.)

explanation.why_correct: Password (know) + token (have) and fingerprint (are) + smart card (have) each combine different factor types—true MFA.

why_others_are_wrong.B: Password + PIN are both knowledge factors (Type 1)—not MFA.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Two fingerprints are both Type 3—not MFA.

questions.exam_reasoning: Identifies genuine multi-factor combinations.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 5 > Authentication Mechanisms > Types of Authentication Factors

questions.question: Directory services (such as those queried by LDAP) primarily provide:

options.label: A
options.text: A method to physically destroy hard drives

options.label: C
options.text: A centralized store of identity and resource information for authentication/authorization

explanation.why_correct: Directory services centrally store identities, groups, and resource information, supporting authentication and authorization decisions.

why_others_are_wrong.A: Drive destruction is a sanitization activity.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Generator control is a power-management function.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests the centralized identity-store role of directory services.

questions.question: RADIUS is commonly used to provide centralized AAA for:

options.label: A
options.text: Encrypting data at rest on servers

options.label: C
options.text: Translating private IPs to public IPs

explanation.why_correct: RADIUS centralizes authentication/authorization/accounting for remote and network access such as VPN and 802.1X Wi-Fi.

why_others_are_wrong.A: Data-at-rest encryption is a separate control.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Fire suppression is a physical control.
why_others_are_wrong.C: IP translation is NAT.

questions.question: Single Sign-On (SSO) primarily allows a user to:

options.label: A
options.text: Use a different password for every application

options.label: C
options.text: Encrypt all of their files automatically

options.label: D
options.text: Authenticate once and gain access to multiple systems without re-entering credentials

explanation.why_correct: SSO lets a user authenticate a single time and then access multiple connected systems without repeatedly entering credentials.

why_others_are_wrong.A: Separate passwords per app is the opposite of SSO.
why_others_are_wrong.B: SSO still requires authentication—just once.
why_others_are_wrong.C: File encryption is unrelated to SSO.

questions.exam_reasoning: Recall of the SSO single-authentication benefit.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 5 > Authentication Mechanisms > Single Sign On

questions.question: A company implements SSO across all internal applications. What is the PRIMARY security drawback the team must mitigate?

options.label: A
options.text: Users must remember dozens of separate passwords

options.label: B
options.text: It makes auditing user activity impossible

options.label: C
options.text: Applications can no longer be accessed at all

options.label: D
options.text: If the single credential is compromised, the attacker can reach all connected systems

explanation.why_correct: SSO concentrates risk: a compromised single credential unlocks every connected system, so it must be paired with strong authentication (e.g., MFA) and monitoring.

why_others_are_wrong.A: SSO reduces the number of passwords—it does not increase them.
why_others_are_wrong.C: SSO enables, not prevents, application access.
why_others_are_wrong.B: SSO does not make auditing impossible; centralized logging is still possible.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests the single-point-of-compromise drawback of SSO.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 5 > Authentication Mechanisms > Single Sign On

questions.question: Which control BEST mitigates the concentrated risk of SSO?

options.label: A
options.text: Using one shared SSO account for the whole team

options.label: B
options.text: Requiring multi-factor authentication for the SSO login

options.label: D
options.text: Disabling logging on the identity provider

explanation.why_correct: Because SSO concentrates access behind one login, protecting that login with MFA substantially reduces the impact of a stolen password.

why_others_are_wrong.D: Disabling logging removes the visibility needed to detect abuse.
why_others_are_wrong.A: A shared account destroys accountability and worsens risk.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Removing timeouts leaves sessions open to hijacking.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps SSO risk mitigation to MFA.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 5 > Authentication Mechanisms > Single Sign On

questions.question: The Kerberos Key Distribution Center (KDC) is composed of which two services?

options.label: A
options.text: Authentication Server (AS) and Ticket Granting Service (TGS)

options.label: B
options.text: Policy Engine and Policy Enforcement Point

explanation.why_correct: The KDC contains the Authentication Server (AS), which issues TGTs, and the Ticket Granting Service (TGS), which issues service tickets.

why_others_are_wrong.D: IdP/SP are SAML federation roles.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Resource Owner/Server are OAuth roles.
why_others_are_wrong.B: PE/PEP are Zero Trust components.

questions.exam_reasoning: Recall of the KDC = AS + TGS.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 5 > Authentication Mechanisms > Kerberos

questions.question: Order the steps of the Kerberos authentication flow. (Provide the option labels in order.)

options.label: B
options.text: Client uses the Service Ticket to access the service

options.label: C
options.text: Client presents the TGT to the Ticket Granting Service (TGS)

options.label: D
options.text: AS issues a Ticket Granting Ticket (TGT)

options.label: E
options.text: Client authenticates to the Authentication Server (AS)

explanation.why_correct: The client authenticates to the AS, receives a TGT, presents the TGT to the TGS, receives a Service Ticket, and uses it to access the target service.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests the ordered Kerberos ticket flow.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 5 > Authentication Mechanisms > Kerberos Operation Flow

questions.question: In Kerberos, a Ticket Granting Ticket (TGT) is used by the client to:

options.label: A
options.text: Directly decrypt the target server's files

options.label: C
options.text: Request service tickets from the Ticket Granting Service without re-entering the password

explanation.why_correct: After authenticating, the client holds a TGT that it presents to the TGS to obtain service tickets, enabling SSO without re-authenticating each time.

why_others_are_wrong.A: A TGT does not decrypt server files directly.
why_others_are_wrong.D: IP assignment is DHCP's function.
why_others_are_wrong.B: A TGT does not disable the KDC.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests the TGT's role in obtaining service tickets.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 5 > Authentication Mechanisms > Tickets

questions.question: In a Kerberos deployment, the KDC becomes unavailable. What is the MOST direct consequence, and what design lesson does it illustrate?

options.label: A
options.text: Authentication fails (Kerberos fails secure); the KDC is a single point of failure that needs redundancy

options.label: C
options.text: Passwords are exposed in cleartext to all users

options.label: D
options.text: All users automatically gain administrator rights

explanation.why_correct: If the KDC is down/compromised, Kerberos fails secure (access is denied), making the KDC a critical single point of failure that should be made redundant and time-synchronized.

why_others_are_wrong.D: KDC failure denies access; it does not grant admin rights.
why_others_are_wrong.B: KDC failure does not delete files.
why_others_are_wrong.C: KDC failure does not expose passwords in cleartext.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests the KDC single-point-of-failure and fail-secure behavior.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 5 > Authentication Mechanisms > Kerberos Operation Flow

questions.question: Why must all systems in a Kerberos realm keep their clocks synchronized?

options.label: A
options.text: It is required to assign MAC addresses

options.label: B
options.text: Kerberos tickets are time-stamped; significant clock skew causes valid tickets to be rejected

explanation.why_correct: Kerberos uses time-stamped tickets (and tolerates only small skew) to resist replay; if clocks drift too far, authentication fails.

why_others_are_wrong.D: Time sync does not increase bandwidth.
why_others_are_wrong.A: MAC assignment is hardware-based, not time-driven.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Time sync does not encrypt databases.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests the time-synchronization dependency of Kerberos.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 5 > Authentication Mechanisms > Kerberos Operation Flow

questions.question: A Kerberoasting attack works by:

options.label: C
options.text: Requesting service tickets and cracking their hashes offline to recover service-account passwords

options.label: D
options.text: Flooding the network with ICMP echo replies

explanation.why_correct: Kerberoasting requests service tickets (encrypted with the service account's key) and cracks the hashes offline to recover the service account's password.

why_others_are_wrong.D: ICMP echo flooding is a Smurf/DoS attack.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Stealing a smart card is a possession-factor theft, not Kerberoasting.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Unsolicited Bluetooth messages are bluejacking.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps offline service-ticket cracking to Kerberoasting.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 5 > Authentication Mechanisms > Kerberos Operation Flow

questions.question: Match each Kerberos element (1-4) to its role (A-D).

options.label: A
options.text: Issues service tickets when presented a valid TGT

options.label: B
options.text: Verifies initial credentials and issues a TGT

options.label: C
options.text: Proves the client authenticated, used to request service tickets

options.label: D
options.text: Presented to a target service to gain access

explanation.why_correct: AS → verifies credentials/issues TGT (B); TGS → issues service tickets (A); TGT → proves authentication, requests service tickets (D); Service Ticket → presented to the target service (C).

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests mapping of Kerberos components to their roles.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 5 > Authentication Mechanisms > Kerberos

questions.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes OAuth 2.0 from OpenID Connect (OIDC)?

options.label: A
options.text: OAuth 2.0 is for authentication; OIDC is only for encryption

options.label: B
options.text: OIDC is older than OAuth and replaced it

options.label: C
options.text: OAuth 2.0 is for delegated authorization; OIDC adds an identity (authentication) layer on top of OAuth 2.0

options.label: D
options.text: They are unrelated and never used together

explanation.why_correct: OAuth 2.0 handles delegated authorization (granting access via tokens); OIDC builds an authentication/identity layer on top of OAuth 2.0 (using REST/JSON, JWTs).

why_others_are_wrong.A: OAuth is authorization-focused; OIDC adds authentication, not encryption only.
why_others_are_wrong.D: OIDC is built directly on OAuth 2.0—they are closely related.
why_others_are_wrong.B: OIDC came after and extends OAuth 2.0; it did not replace it.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests the authorization (OAuth) vs authentication (OIDC) distinction.

questions.question: A user lets a photo-printing app access their cloud photos WITHOUT sharing their cloud password, by granting a scoped access token. Which standard enables this delegated access?

why_others_are_wrong.A: WEP is a wireless encryption protocol.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Kerberoasting is an attack technique.
why_others_are_wrong.C: CPTED is a physical site-design strategy.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps password-less delegated access to OAuth 2.0.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 5 > Authentication Mechanisms > OAuth and OIDC

why_others_are_wrong.C: File encryption is unrelated to OpenID.

why_others_are_wrong.D: Packet routing is a network function.

questions.question: In the OAuth framework, the application requesting access to protected resources on the user's behalf is the:

explanation.why_correct: The OAuth client is the application requesting access; the resource owner is the user, the resource server hosts the data, and the authorization server issues tokens.

why_others_are_wrong.C: The resource owner is the user who owns the data and grants access.
why_others_are_wrong.B: The resource server hosts the protected resources.
why_others_are_wrong.A: The authorization server issues access tokens.

questions.question: In enterprise web SSO, SAML is commonly used to:

options.text: Pass authentication/authorization assertions from an identity provider to web applications

why_others_are_wrong.A: File encryption is a separate control.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Fire suppression is a physical control.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Backup power is a UPS/generator function.

questions.question: OpenID Connect commonly conveys identity claims using which token format?

questions.question: A credential management system (password manager) primarily helps users by:

questions.question: A "credential vault" within a CMS is best described as:

options.text: A secured, encrypted store that holds credentials and secrets

questions.question: An organization adopts a centralized credential vault. What is the KEY risk that must be tightly controlled?

questions.question: Just-In-Time (JIT) access reduces standing privilege by:

options.label: B

options.text: Granting elevated access only for the time it is needed, then automatically revoking it

options.label: D
options.text: Sharing one admin account among the team

explanation.why_correct: JIT access provisions elevated rights only when needed and for a limited window (often via ephemeral accounts/temporary elevation), shrinking the attack surface of standing privilege.

why_others_are_wrong.B: Permanent admin rights are exactly what JIT avoids.
why_others_are_wrong.A: JIT complements, not eliminates, access reviews.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Shared admin accounts destroy accountability.

questions.question: An "ephemeral account" used in JIT access is one that:

options.text: Exists only temporarily for a specific task and is removed afterward

why_others_are_wrong.C: They are single-purpose and temporary, not shared indefinitely.

questions.question: Privileged Access Management (PAM) focuses primarily on:

why_others_are_wrong.C: Fire suppression is a physical control.
