why_others_are_wrong.D: WEP is a wireless cipher, not an authorization framework.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Kerberoasting is an attack and CPTED is physical design.
why_others_are_wrong.B: RADIUS is network AAA and degaussing destroys media—neither fits.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps enterprise SSO to SAML and delegated authorization to OAuth.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 5 > Authentication Mechanisms > OAuth and OIDC

questions.question: A security strength of Kerberos is that it:

options.label: A
options.text: Transmits passwords in cleartext for speed

options.label: B
options.text: Stores all credentials on every client

options.label: C
options.text: Provides mutual authentication and avoids sending passwords across the network

options.label: D
options.text: Eliminates the need for any time source

explanation.why_correct: Kerberos supports mutual authentication and uses tickets/keys so user passwords are not transmitted across the network in the clear.

why_others_are_wrong.A: Kerberos specifically avoids sending cleartext passwords.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Kerberos depends on synchronized time.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Credentials are managed by the KDC, not stored on every client.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests the no-cleartext-password and mutual-auth strengths of Kerberos.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 5 > Authentication Mechanisms > Kerberos

questions.question: Which is a sound security practice when deploying a credential management system?

options.label: A
options.text: Allow anonymous access to the vault

options.label: B
options.text: Store the master password on a public web page

options.label: C
options.text: Disable encryption to speed up retrieval

options.label: D
options.text: Protect the vault with strong authentication (e.g., MFA) and restrict/monitor access

explanation.why_correct: The vault holds many secrets, so it must be protected with strong authentication, least-privilege access, encryption, and monitoring.

why_others_are_wrong.B: Publishing the master password defeats the vault entirely.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Disabling encryption exposes all stored secrets.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Anonymous access would expose every stored credential.

questions.exam_reasoning: Identifies sound CMS protection practices.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 5 > Authentication Mechanisms > Credential Management Systems

questions.question: OAuth 2.0 authorizes a client to access resources by issuing it a(n):

options.label: D
options.text: Access token with a defined scope

explanation.why_correct: OAuth issues scoped access tokens that the client presents to the resource server to access only the permitted resources.

why_others_are_wrong.B: Service tickets belong to Kerberos, not OAuth.
why_others_are_wrong.C: An LDAP DN names a directory entry.
why_others_are_wrong.A: A WPA2 PSK is a wireless key.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps OAuth scoped access to access tokens.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 5 > Authentication Mechanisms > OAuth and OIDC

questions.question: Besides the security risk, which is a noted practical DRAWBACK of implementing SSO?

options.label: B
options.text: It cannot be combined with MFA

options.label: C
options.text: Integration complexity and expense across many applications

options.label: D
options.text: It removes the need for an identity provider

explanation.why_correct: SSO can be costly and complex to integrate across diverse applications, which is a practical drawback noted in the guide.

why_others_are_wrong.A: SSO reduces the number of passwords.
why_others_are_wrong.B: SSO can and should be combined with MFA.
why_others_are_wrong.D: SSO relies on an identity provider, not removes it.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests the integration cost/complexity drawback of SSO.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 5 > Authentication Mechanisms > Single Sign On

questions.question: In Discretionary Access Control (DAC), access decisions are based on:

options.label: B
options.text: The object OWNER granting permissions to subjects, typically via an ACL

options.label: C
options.text: Security labels and clearances enforced by a central authority

explanation.why_correct: In DAC, the object owner determines who may access the object, usually through an Access Control List (ACL); it is flexible but offers weaker, identity-based control.

why_others_are_wrong.C: Labels/clearances enforced centrally describe MAC.
why_others_are_wrong.D: A real-time risk score describes risk-based access control.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Port/protocol rules describe rule-based access control.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps owner-set, ACL-based access to DAC.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 5 > Access and Authorization > Discretionary Access Control (DAC)

questions.question: Mandatory Access Control (MAC) enforces access using:

options.label: A
options.text: A list of allowed TCP ports

options.label: B
options.text: The discretion of the individual data owner

options.label: C
options.text: Security labels on subjects and objects compared against the subject's clearance

explanation.why_correct: MAC is non-discretionary: access is determined by comparing security labels/classifications on objects against the subject's clearance, common in military/highly sensitive environments.

why_others_are_wrong.B: Owner discretion describes DAC.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Role/group membership describes RBAC.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Allowed ports describe rule-based access control.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps label/clearance enforcement to MAC.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 5 > Access and Authorization > Mandatory Access Control (MAC)

questions.question: Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) grants access based on:

options.label: A
options.text: A subject's assigned role or group, helping reduce privilege creep

explanation.why_correct: RBAC assigns permissions to roles/groups and users inherit them via role membership, streamlining administration and reducing privilege creep—useful for high-turnover environments.

why_others_are_wrong.D: Labels/clearances describe MAC.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Owner discretion describes DAC.
why_others_are_wrong.C: A geolocation risk score describes risk-based access control.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps role/group-based access to RBAC.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 5 > Access and Authorization > Role-Based Access Control (RBAC)

questions.question: Attribute-Based Access Control (ABAC) makes decisions based on:

options.label: A
options.text: Multiple attributes of the subject, object, action, and environment

explanation.why_correct: ABAC (also called policy-based access control) evaluates combinations of subject, object, action, and environmental attributes (e.g., clearance, department, time, IP), enabling fine-grained policies often via XACML.

why_others_are_wrong.D: Owner-only preference describes DAC.
why_others_are_wrong.B: A single role describes RBAC, which is coarser than ABAC.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Port-only decisions describe rule-based access control.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps multi-attribute, fine-grained decisions to ABAC.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 5 > Access and Authorization > Attribute-Based Access Control (ABAC)

questions.question: Rule-based access control, as used in devices like firewalls, grants or denies access based on:

options.label: D
options.text: Predefined rules such as port number and protocol

explanation.why_correct: Rule-based access control applies predefined rules/restrictions (e.g., allow HTTP on port 80) regardless of user identity, common in firewalls and IPS.

why_others_are_wrong.B: Biometric templates relate to authentication, not rule-based ACLs.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Owner discretion describes DAC.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Job-title/role-based access is RBAC.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps predefined port/protocol rules to rule-based access control.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 5 > Access and Authorization > Rule-Based Access Control

questions.question: A user logs in from an unrecognized IP on an untrusted network, so the system requires additional authentication factors before granting access. Which access control model is this?

explanation.why_correct: Risk-based (RAdAC) access control dynamically adjusts requirements based on a calculated risk level (device, location, sensitivity), e.g., demanding MFA for higher-risk logins.

why_others_are_wrong.C: DAC relies on owner-set permissions, not dynamic risk.
why_others_are_wrong.A: MAC uses static labels/clearances.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Rule-based uses fixed rules, not adaptive risk scoring.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps adaptive, risk-driven authentication to risk-based access control.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 5 > Access and Authorization > Risk-Based Access Control

questions.question: A defense agency must enforce that data classified "Top Secret" is only accessible to subjects with Top Secret clearance, with no owner discretion allowed. Which model is MOST appropriate?

explanation.why_correct: MAC enforces non-discretionary access using labels/clearances—ideal for classified environments where owners cannot override the policy.

why_others_are_wrong.A: DAC allows owner discretion, which the requirement forbids.
why_others_are_wrong.C: RBAC groups by role but does not enforce clearance/label dominance like MAC.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Rule-based controls (e.g., port rules) do not enforce classification clearance.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps clearance-enforced, non-discretionary classification to MAC.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 5 > Access and Authorization > Mandatory Access Control (MAC)

questions.question: A call center with very high staff turnover wants to simplify granting and revoking access as employees join and leave. Which access control model BEST fits?

options.label: A
options.text: MAC — assign clearances and labels to every file

options.label: B
options.text: DAC — let each employee set their own permissions

options.label: C
options.text: RBAC — assign access to roles, then add/remove users from roles

options.label: D
options.text: Risk-based — recompute risk on every keystroke

explanation.why_correct: RBAC streamlines administration in high-turnover environments: access is tied to roles, so onboarding/offboarding is just role assignment/removal.

why_others_are_wrong.B: DAC self-set permissions would be chaotic and inconsistent at scale.
why_others_are_wrong.A: MAC labeling every file is heavy and aimed at classified data, not call-center turnover.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Per-keystroke risk scoring is unnecessary overhead for this need.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps high-turnover administration efficiency to RBAC.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 5 > Access and Authorization > Role-Based Access Control (RBAC)

questions.question: Match each access control model (1-4) to the basis for its access decisions (A-D).

options.label: D
options.text: Security labels/clearances set by a central authority

explanation.why_correct: DAC → owner discretion/ACLs (B); MAC → labels/clearances (A); RBAC → role/group membership (D); ABAC → multiple attributes (C).

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests mapping of access control models to their decision basis.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 5 > Access and Authorization > Access Control Models

questions.question: A noted security weakness of DAC compared to MAC is that DAC:

options.label: A
options.text: Is only usable on wireless networks

options.label: B
options.text: Cannot use access control lists at all

options.label: C
options.text: Relies on individual owners' discretion, making consistent, fine-grained control harder to guarantee

explanation.why_correct: Because DAC delegates access decisions to object owners, enforcement can be inconsistent and harder to control centrally—weaker than label-driven MAC for sensitive data.

why_others_are_wrong.B: DAC specifically uses ACLs.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Clearances are a MAC concept, not required by DAC.
why_others_are_wrong.A: DAC is not limited to wireless networks.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests the discretion-driven weakness of DAC.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 5 > Access and Authorization > Discretionary Access Control (DAC)

questions.question: In non-discretionary access control, access rights are determined by:

options.label: A
options.text: A central authority or policy, not the individual object owner

options.label: C
options.text: The current temperature of the server room

options.label: D
options.text: Each user for their own files

explanation.why_correct: Non-discretionary models (e.g., MAC, RBAC) have a central authority/policy set access rights, rather than leaving them to object owners (DAC).

why_others_are_wrong.D: Per-user discretion is DAC, which is discretionary.
why_others_are_wrong.B: MAC-address-only decisions are a Layer 2 filter, not this concept.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Room temperature is an environmental control.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests the central-authority basis of non-discretionary control.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 5 > Access and Authorization > Non-Discretionary Access Control

questions.question: Which TWO are categories of attributes that ABAC can evaluate? (Select TWO.)

options.label: B
options.text: The font used in the document

options.label: C
options.text: The color of the user's desk

explanation.why_correct: ABAC evaluates subject, object, action, and environmental attributes; clearance/department (subject) and time/IP (environmental) are valid examples.

why_others_are_wrong.B: Document font is not an access-control attribute.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Desk color is irrelevant to access decisions.

questions.exam_reasoning: Identifies legitimate ABAC attribute categories.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 5 > Access and Authorization > Attribute-Based Access Control (ABAC)

questions.question: The principle of "implicit deny" means that:

options.label: B
options.text: Access is allowed by default unless explicitly denied

options.label: C
options.text: Logging is turned off by default

options.label: D
options.text: Access is denied by default unless it is explicitly granted

explanation.why_correct: Implicit deny ("permit by exception, deny by default") denies any access not explicitly allowed, a secure default.

why_others_are_wrong.B: Allow-by-default is the opposite (and insecure) approach.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Implicit deny restricts, not grants, broad access.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Implicit deny concerns access, not logging configuration.

questions.exam_reasoning: Recall of the deny-by-default principle.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 5 > Access and Authorization > Access Authorization

questions.question: In the guide's authorization terminology, "privileges" are best defined as:

options.label: A
options.text: Only the subject's ability to access an object

options.label: B
options.text: The combination of a subject's permissions and rights

options.label: C
options.text: A list of all denied users

options.label: D
options.text: Only the subject's authority to perform specific actions

explanation.why_correct: Privileges are the combination of permissions (ability to access an object) and rights (authority to perform actions).

why_others_are_wrong.A: Ability to access an object alone is a permission.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Authority to perform actions alone is a right.
why_others_are_wrong.C: A deny list is not the definition of privileges.

questions.exam_reasoning: Distinguishes privileges from permissions and rights.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 5 > Access and Authorization > Access Authorization

questions.subtopic: Access control matrix vs capability table
questions.question: How does a capability table differ from an access control matrix?

options.label: A
options.text: A capability table is object-focused and a matrix is subject-focused

options.label: B
options.text: They are identical in every way

options.label: C
options.text: A capability table is a physical security barrier

options.label: D
options.text: A capability table is subject-focused (lists what a subject can access), while an ACL/matrix is object-focused

explanation.why_correct: A capability table lists a subject's capabilities (subject-focused); an access control list/matrix is organized by object (object-focused). They are complementary views.

why_others_are_wrong.A: This reverses the focus of each.
why_others_are_wrong.B: They present different (subject vs object) views.
why_others_are_wrong.C: A capability table is a logical construct, not a physical barrier.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests subject-focused (capability) vs object-focused (matrix/ACL).

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 5 > Access and Authorization > Access Authorization

questions.question: A database hides specific salary columns from users not in HR based on the data being viewed. This is an example of which control?

options.label: B
options.text: Context-dependent control (based on the sequence/situation of actions)

options.label: C
options.text: Content-dependent control (based on the type/content of the object)

explanation.why_correct: Content-dependent controls restrict access based on the actual content/type of the object (e.g., specific sensitive columns), independent of the request sequence.

why_others_are_wrong.B: Context-dependent controls depend on the situation/sequence of actions, not the data content itself.
why_others_are_wrong.D: A firewall rule filters network traffic, not database column content.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Physical access control governs facility entry, not data columns.

questions.exam_reasoning: Distinguishes content-dependent from context-dependent controls.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 5 > Access and Authorization > Content-Dependent vs. Context-Dependent Controls

questions.question: A constrained interface restricts access by:

options.label: C
options.text: Limiting the actions/options available based on the subject's privilege level

explanation.why_correct: A constrained interface only exposes the functions/options a subject is privileged to use, implementing least privilege at the interface.

why_others_are_wrong.A: Connection encryption is a transport control, not interface constraint.
why_others_are_wrong.D: IP assignment is DHCP's function.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Locking a rack is a physical control.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps privilege-limited interfaces to constrained interfaces.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 5 > Access and Authorization > Access Authorization

questions.question: Separation of duties as an authorization principle is designed to:

options.label: A
options.text: Divide critical tasks among multiple people to prevent any one person having excessive control

options.label: B
options.text: Remove the need for least privilege

options.label: C
options.text: Allow users to approve their own requests

options.label: D
options.text: Give one administrator complete control for efficiency

explanation.why_correct: Separation of duties splits sensitive tasks so no single individual can complete a critical process alone, reducing fraud and error.

why_others_are_wrong.D: Concentrating control in one person defeats separation of duties.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Self-approval undermines the control.
why_others_are_wrong.B: SoD complements, not replaces, least privilege.

questions.exam_reasoning: Recall of separation of duties.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 5 > Access and Authorization > Authorization Principles

questions.question: Least privilege in authorization means providing subjects with:

options.label: B
options.text: The maximum access in case it is needed later

options.label: C
options.text: Access to all data in the organization

options.label: D
options.text: Only the access rights necessary to perform their role

explanation.why_correct: Least privilege grants only the access necessary for a subject's duties, limiting the impact of compromise or misuse.

why_others_are_wrong.B: Granting extra "just in case" access violates least privilege.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Default admin rights are excessive.
why_others_are_wrong.C: All-data access ignores need-to-know and least privilege.

questions.exam_reasoning: Recall of least privilege.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 5 > Access and Authorization > Authorization Principles

questions.question: A user has the technical permission to open a shared folder but should not see one specific file unrelated to their duties. Restricting that file enforces:

explanation.why_correct: Need to know restricts access to specific information to only those who require it for their duties, even where broader permissions exist.

why_others_are_wrong.B: "Implicit allow" is insecure and not the principle here.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Mandatory vacation is a fraud-detection control.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Open design is a secure-design principle, not access scoping.

questions.exam_reasoning: Distinguishes need-to-know from least privilege.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 5 > Access and Authorization > Authorization Principles

questions.question: Which TWO are authorization principles emphasized in the guide? (Select TWO.)

explanation.why_correct: Separation of duties and least privilege (with need-to-know) are core authorization principles.

why_others_are_wrong.D: Security through obscurity is discouraged, not an authorization principle.
why_others_are_wrong.B: "Implicit allow" is insecure; the secure default is implicit deny.

questions.exam_reasoning: Identifies sound authorization principles.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 5 > Access and Authorization > Authorization Principles

questions.question: Accountability in access management ensures that:

options.label: B
options.text: Subjects can be held responsible for their actions, supporting non-repudiation

options.label: D
options.text: All data is encrypted at rest

explanation.why_correct: Accountability tracks and verifies subjects' actions so they can be held responsible, supporting non-repudiation.

why_others_are_wrong.D: Data-at-rest encryption is a separate control.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Accountability does not guarantee uptime.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Plaintext password storage is an insecure practice, not accountability.

questions.exam_reasoning: Recall of accountability and its link to non-repudiation.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 5 > Access and Authorization > Accountability

questions.question: Which mechanism is MOST fundamental to implementing accountability?

explanation.why_correct: Logging and auditing of actions are fundamental to accountability—recording who did what, when, to support investigation and non-repudiation.

why_others_are_wrong.C: Disabling accounts prevents work, not enables accountability.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Removing the identity provider would undermine authentication and tracking.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Disabling encryption is unrelated and insecure.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps accountability to logging/auditing.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 5 > Access and Authorization > Implementing Accountability

questions.question: An attacker who gains admin access tries to delete the audit logs to hide their actions. Which control BEST preserves accountability?

options.label: B
options.text: Storing logs on the same account the admin controls

options.label: C
options.text: Allowing all users to edit logs

options.label: D
options.text: Protecting logs from tampering (e.g., write-once/remote log storage with restricted access)

explanation.why_correct: Protecting logs from tampering—e.g., forwarding to a secured/append-only remote log store with strict access—preserves accountability even if an endpoint is compromised.

why_others_are_wrong.B: Storing logs where the admin can alter them defeats accountability.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Disabling logging creates blind spots attackers exploit.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Allowing anyone to edit logs destroys their integrity.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests protecting log integrity to preserve accountability.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 5 > Access and Authorization > Implementing Accountability

questions.question: Accountability supports non-repudiation by:

options.label: B
options.text: Suppressing fires in the data center

options.label: D
options.text: Linking actions to authenticated subjects so they cannot credibly deny performing them

explanation.why_correct: By tying logged actions to authenticated identities, accountability prevents subjects from denying actions they performed (non-repudiation).

why_others_are_wrong.C: WAN encryption is unrelated to non-repudiation linkage.
why_others_are_wrong.A: IP assignment is DHCP's function.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Fire suppression is a physical control.

questions.exam_reasoning: Connects accountability to non-repudiation.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 5 > Access and Authorization > Key Benefits

questions.question: A session timeout improves security by:

options.label: A
options.text: Automatically ending an inactive session and requiring re-authentication

explanation.why_correct: Session timeouts end inactive sessions after a set period, reducing the risk of an unattended, still-authenticated session being hijacked.

why_others_are_wrong.C: A timeout ends a session; it does not disable the account.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Timeouts do not encrypt files.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Timeouts do not assign IP addresses.

questions.exam_reasoning: Recall of session timeout purpose.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 5 > Access and Authorization > Session Management

questions.question: A session ID is used to:

options.label: A
options.text: Bind a user's authenticated credentials to an active session

explanation.why_correct: A session ID ties the user's credentials/state to an active session, and must be protected (e.g., against hijacking/fixation).

why_others_are_wrong.D: Disk encryption is a separate control.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Backup power is a UPS/generator function.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Name resolution is DNS.

questions.exam_reasoning: Recall of the session ID purpose.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 5 > Access and Authorization > Session Management

questions.question: To reduce the risk of session hijacking on a web application, which combination is MOST effective?

options.label: A
options.text: Reuse the same session ID for all users

options.label: B
options.text: Embed the user password in every URL

options.label: D
options.text: Use unpredictable session IDs over TLS and enforce idle/absolute session timeouts

explanation.why_correct: Strong, random session IDs transmitted over TLS, combined with idle/absolute timeouts, significantly reduce hijacking/fixation risk.

why_others_are_wrong.B: Putting passwords in URLs exposes them in logs/history.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Reusing one session ID for all users is catastrophic.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Disabling HTTPS exposes session tokens to interception.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests layered defenses against session hijacking.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 5 > Access and Authorization > Session Management

questions.question: In access control terminology, a "subject" is:

options.label: D
options.text: An active entity (user, program, or process) that requests access to an object

explanation.why_correct: A subject is the active entity (user, program, script, service) that acts on an object (the passive resource being accessed).

why_others_are_wrong.B: A passive resource being accessed is the object, not the subject.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Fire suppression is a physical control.
why_others_are_wrong.A: A generator provides backup power.

questions.exam_reasoning: Distinguishes subject (active) from object (passive).

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 5 > Access and Authorization > Subjects and Objects in Logical Access

questions.question: A web server requests data from a database, then returns it to a user's browser. Regarding the database transaction, the web server is acting as the ____.

options.label: B
options.text: Subject (it is the active entity requesting the object/data)

explanation.why_correct: Subject/object roles are relative: when the web server requests data from the database, the server is the active subject and the database is the object. Roles interchange based on the access.

why_others_are_wrong.A: In this transaction the database (not the web server) is the passive object.
why_others_are_wrong.C: A reference monitor mediates access; it is not the requesting server here.
why_others_are_wrong.D: An identity provider issues identity assertions, unrelated to this DB request.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests that subject/object roles interchange by context.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 5 > Access and Authorization > Subjects and Objects in Logical Access

questions.question: The goals of controlling logical access align directly with which security model?

explanation.why_correct: Logical access control aims to prevent unauthorized disclosure (confidentiality), maintain authorized-only changes (integrity), and ensure availability for authorized subjects—the CIA triad.

why_others_are_wrong.B: The fire triangle is a physical-safety concept.
why_others_are_wrong.D: The OSI model describes networking layers.
why_others_are_wrong.C: The TCP handshake establishes a connection.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps logical-access goals to the CIA triad.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 5 > Access and Authorization > Goals in Controlling Access

questions.question: DAC commonly tracks which subjects may access an object using a(n):

explanation.why_correct: DAC uses Access Control Lists (ACLs) to record which subjects have which permissions on an object.

why_others_are_wrong.A: A fire suppression plan is a physical-safety document.
why_others_are_wrong.D: A subnet mask defines network ranges.
why_others_are_wrong.C: A UPS battery provides backup power.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps DAC permission tracking to ACLs.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 5 > Access and Authorization > Discretionary Access Control (DAC)

questions.question: MAC is most commonly used in environments handling:

options.label: A
options.text: Highly sensitive data such as national security, PII, or PHI

options.label: C
options.text: Disposable test data with no value

explanation.why_correct: MAC's rigid label/clearance enforcement suits highly sensitive environments (military/government, regulated PII/PHI).

why_others_are_wrong.D: Public brochures need little access control.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Guest Wi-Fi does not require MAC labeling.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Disposable test data does not warrant MAC overhead.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps MAC to highly sensitive environments.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 5 > Access and Authorization > Mandatory Access Control (MAC)

questions.question: An access control list (ACL) attached to a file is an example of which type of access view?

options.label: A
options.text: Object-focused (lists which subjects can access the object)

explanation.why_correct: An ACL is organized by the object, listing which subjects have which permissions on it (object-focused); a capability table is subject-focused.

why_others_are_wrong.D: A subject-focused list is a capability table, not an ACL.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Risk-based scoring is a dynamic model, not an ACL view.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Biometric enrollment is an authentication process.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps ACLs to the object-focused view.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 5 > Access and Authorization > Access Authorization

questions.question: Besides assigning responsibility, robust accountability/auditing can also:

options.label: B
options.text: Reveal design vulnerabilities that allow unauthorized actions

explanation.why_correct: Reviewing accountability data can expose gaps/vulnerabilities in system design that permit unauthorized actions, informing improvements.

why_others_are_wrong.A: Auditing complements, not replaces, authentication.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Auditing does not encrypt data.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Backups remain necessary for availability.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests the design-insight benefit of accountability.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 5 > Access and Authorization > Key Benefits

questions.question: A long-tenured employee has accumulated access from every past role (privilege creep). Which TWO practices BEST prevent this? (Select TWO.)

options.label: B
options.text: Granting permanent administrator rights to all staff

options.label: D
options.text: Role-based access tied to current duties, removing old access on transfer

explanation.why_correct: Periodic access reviews and RBAC tied to current roles (removing old access at transfer) prevent the accumulation of unneeded access (privilege creep).

why_others_are_wrong.C: Disabling logging removes visibility and worsens security.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Permanent admin rights for all is excessive standing privilege, the opposite of the goal.

questions.exam_reasoning: Identifies practices that prevent privilege creep.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 5 > Access and Authorization > Role-Based Access Control (RBAC)

questions.question: In authorization terms, a "right" refers to a subject's:

options.label: D
options.text: Authority to conduct specific actions (e.g., shut down a system)

explanation.why_correct: A right is the authority to perform specific actions; permissions concern access to objects, and privileges combine the two.

why_others_are_wrong.C: Office location is not an authorization right.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Browser choice is irrelevant to authorization rights.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Bandwidth allocation is a network resource matter.

questions.exam_reasoning: Recall of "rights" in authorization.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 5 > Access and Authorization > Access Authorization

questions.question: Rule-based access control is MOST commonly seen in which type of device?

explanation.why_correct: Rule-based access control (allow/deny by predefined rules like port/protocol) is characteristic of firewalls and IPS.

why_others_are_wrong.A: Fingerprint readers perform biometric authentication.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Generators provide backup power.
why_others_are_wrong.D: HVAC units manage environment, not access rules.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps rule-based control to firewalls/IPS.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 5 > Access and Authorization > Rule-Based Access Control

questions.question: A new application is configured so that any access not explicitly permitted is blocked. A user with no assigned permissions tries to open a record and is denied. This reflects which principle?

explanation.why_correct: Blocking anything not explicitly permitted is implicit deny ("permit by exception, deny by default")—a secure default.

why_others_are_wrong.A: Implicit allow would have granted the access.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Mandatory vacation is a fraud-detection control.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Privilege creep is accumulation of excess access, not a default-deny outcome.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps default-blocking behavior to implicit deny.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 5 > Access and Authorization > Access Authorization

questions.question: Compared to RBAC, ABAC provides FINER-grained control primarily because it can:

options.label: A
options.text: Eliminate the need for any policy

options.label: B
options.text: Only ever consider the user's role

options.label: D
options.text: Factor in many attributes (e.g., time, location, device) beyond a single role

explanation.why_correct: ABAC evaluates multiple attributes (subject, object, action, environment), enabling more granular, context-aware decisions than role-only RBAC.

why_others_are_wrong.B: Considering only a role describes RBAC, which is coarser.
why_others_are_wrong.C: ABAC can use object sensitivity as an attribute.
why_others_are_wrong.A: ABAC is policy-driven; it does not remove the need for policy.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests why ABAC is finer-grained than RBAC.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 5 > Access and Authorization > Attribute-Based Access Control (ABAC)

questions.question: Which activity BEST demonstrates accountability in action?

options.label: A
options.text: Logs that record which user accessed and deleted a sensitive file

options.label: C
options.text: A faster internet connection for the office

explanation.why_correct: Recording who accessed/modified/deleted sensitive data is accountability in action—enabling investigation and non-repudiation.

why_others_are_wrong.C: Bandwidth is unrelated to accountability.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Lighting is a physical/CPTED control.
why_others_are_wrong.B: A UPS supports availability, not action attribution.

questions.exam_reasoning: Identifies a concrete accountability example.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 5 > Access and Authorization > Accountability

questions.question: After a session times out due to inactivity, the user must:

options.label: A
options.text: Wait for the network to reboot

options.label: C
options.text: Re-authenticate to start a new session

explanation.why_correct: A timed-out session requires re-authentication before a new session is established, limiting unauthorized use of an abandoned session.

why_others_are_wrong.A: The network does not need to reboot for re-authentication.
why_others_are_wrong.B: No OS reinstall is required.
why_others_are_wrong.D: MAC address changes are unrelated to session re-authentication.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests the re-authentication requirement after timeout.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 5 > Access and Authorization > Session Management

questions.question: The overall purpose of any access control model is to govern:

options.label: A
options.text: The color scheme of the user interface

options.label: B
options.text: The brand of network cabling used

options.label: C
options.text: How a subject is permitted to interact with an object

explanation.why_correct: Access control models define how subjects (users, devices, processes) are authorized to interact with objects (files, services, functions).

why_others_are_wrong.A: UI color is a cosmetic choice.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Cabling brand is a procurement detail.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Seating arrangement is unrelated to logical access control.

questions.exam_reasoning: Recall of the purpose of access control models.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 5 > Access and Authorization > Access Control Models

questions.question: A "permission," in authorization terms, refers to a subject's:

options.label: A
options.text: Authority to perform any action anywhere

explanation.why_correct: A permission is the ability to access an object; combined with rights (authority to act), they form privileges.

why_others_are_wrong.A: Authority to perform actions is a "right," not a permission.
why_others_are_wrong.C: A clearance badge is a physical credential, not the logical permission concept.
why_others_are_wrong.B: A biometric template is authentication data, not a permission.

questions.exam_reasoning: Recall of "permission" in authorization.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 5 > Access and Authorization > Access Authorization

questions.question: Which TWO contextual factors might a risk-based access control system evaluate? (Select TWO.)

explanation.why_correct: Risk-based access control uses contextual data such as device trust and geolocation (plus network attributes and object sensitivity) to calculate risk.

why_others_are_wrong.D: Personal food preferences are irrelevant to access risk.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Wall color is irrelevant to access decisions.

questions.exam_reasoning: Identifies legitimate risk-based contextual factors.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 5 > Access and Authorization > Risk-Based Access Control

questions.question: Logical access control manages a subject's ability to:

options.label: C
options.text: Adjust the thermostat in the lobby

options.label: D
options.text: Open, modify, execute, or delete data and resources

explanation.why_correct: Logical access control governs privileges to open, modify, execute, or delete data/resources, protecting confidentiality, integrity, and availability.

why_others_are_wrong.B: Physical entry is a physical access control.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Thermostat control is an environmental matter.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Parking is a physical/facility concern.

questions.exam_reasoning: Distinguishes logical from physical access control.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 5 > Access and Authorization > Controlling Logical Access

questions.question: A finance process is designed so the person who creates a vendor payment cannot also approve it. This control is:

explanation.why_correct: Requiring different people to create and approve a payment is separation of duties, preventing one individual from completing a sensitive transaction alone.

why_others_are_wrong.D: SSO is an authentication convenience, not a duty split.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Implicit allow is an insecure default, unrelated here.
why_others_are_wrong.B: A session timeout ends inactive sessions; it is not duty separation.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps create-vs-approve separation to separation of duties.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 5 > Access and Authorization > Authorization Principles

questions.question: DAC is often described as "identity-based" access control because access depends on:

options.label: B
options.text: The classification label of the data only

options.label: D
options.text: The identity of the individual subject and the owner's granted permissions

explanation.why_correct: DAC ties access to the subject's identity and the owner-granted permissions (via ACLs), hence "identity-based."

why_others_are_wrong.B: Classification-label enforcement describes MAC.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Network risk scoring describes risk-based access control.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Firewall rule sets describe rule-based access control.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps identity-based access to DAC.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 5 > Access and Authorization > Discretionary Access Control (DAC)

questions.question: To support accountability, access to logs and sensitive files should be governed by:

options.label: C
options.text: A single shared account for convenience

options.label: D
options.text: Strong authentication and least-privilege access controls

explanation.why_correct: Strong authentication and least privilege over logs/sensitive files protect their integrity and ensure actions are attributable—supporting accountability.

why_others_are_wrong.B: Anonymous access destroys attribution.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Shared accounts eliminate individual accountability.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Removing authentication breaks accountability.

questions.exam_reasoning: Connects strong access controls to accountability.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 5 > Access and Authorization > Implementing Accountability
